findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script into sh in Dockerfile build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads and runs whatever the URL serves at build time, as root in the image build. There is no pinned version, checksum or signature. Anyone who controls or compromises that host, DNS or TLS path gets code execution in the build and the shipped image. The build is also not reproducible, because the script content can change between builds. Failure handling is weak too. `-s` hides errors and `-f` is missing, so an HTTP 4xx/5xx error page is passed to `sh`. The default `/bin/sh` has no `pipefail`, so a failed download lets `sh` read empty or partial input and exit 0. The build then succeeds with the intended install silently missing or truncated.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing and returns "" with no explicit default or doc
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault is exported and discards Load's error with `v, _ := Load(key, m)` (src/store.go:16). A missing key returns "", and so does a key present with value "", so callers of this helper cannot tell absent from empty. Load still distinguishes them (src/store.go:10 returns ErrMissing, src/store.go:12 returns nil). The signature has no default parameter and there is no doc comment saying the default is "". Returning the zero value is a common Go pattern, and no caller in the repo uses the helper, so the impact is limited to future external callers. Callers that need to tell the cases apart can still use Load.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent, breaking completion and ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run sent every result synchronously, so when it returned all results had been sent. A caller could then safely `close(results)` or stop reading. Now each send runs in an untracked goroutine (src/worker.go:7-9) and Run returns immediately. A caller that closes `results` after Run returns gets `panic: send on closed channel` from the goroutines still pending. A caller that stops reading leaves one goroutine per job blocked forever on `results <- ...`, which is an unbounded leak for large `jobs`. Run ignores ctx, as it did before, so cancellation cannot unblock those sends. Result order no longer follows the order of `jobs`. Run is exported and its contract that results are delivered by the time it returns is silently dropped. Run has no callers in this repo, so the exposure is to external callers of the exported API.

findings.title: Log accepts a tag parameter but never uses it
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature now promises that callers can attach tag(s) to a log message. The body still runs only `println(message)` and never reads `tag`. A call like `Log("x", "auth")` compiles and looks tagged, but the output is identical to an untagged call. The tag is dropped with no error. Any caller or log consumer relying on tags for filtering or attribution gets nothing.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord uses || and bypasses tenant and admin checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version required both session.isAdmin and a matching tenantId. The new `||` returns true if either holds. A non-admin in the same tenant can now delete any record in that tenant. Any admin, including one from another tenant, can delete records across tenants. This breaks both the admin-only rule and tenant isolation in the one exported function that decides record deletion.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows parse errors and returns defaults, enabling data loss
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch-all at src/settings.ts:14-16 returns { ...DEFAULTS } for malformed JSON, a missing or invalid theme, and a missing or invalid fontSize. Callers can no longer tell a failure from real settings. updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) hits this directly. If the stored settings have a valid theme but fontSize is missing or a string, or the JSON is corrupt, parseSettings returns the defaults. updateFontSize then sets fontSize and calls save(JSON.stringify(...)), which persists theme:"light" and overwrites the user's real theme and any other data. Before this change the error propagated and save was never called, so the stored settings were left alone.

findings.title: buildReport lists artifacts from 'verified' ref but reports builtFrom branch
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` is still the commit resolved from the caller's `branch` (src/report.ts:12). `artifacts` is now computed from `build.ref("verified")` (src/report.ts:13-14), a hardcoded ref that is unrelated to `branch`. Whenever `verified` differs from `branch` (the normal case for any non-verified branch or a branch ahead of verified), the exported BuildReport pairs a commit with another commit's artifacts. Consumers will trust that the artifacts were built from `builtFrom`. The `branch` parameter no longer determines the artifact list. Nothing in the diff says the change is intentional, and no code in the repo uses a 'verified' ref.

findings.title: recentEntries drops the slice and ignores positive limits
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. The new code reverses the array and returns it whole whenever `limit > 0`, so `slice(0, limit)` is gone. The doc comment promises "at most `limit` entries", but `recentEntries(all, 20)` now returns every entry. renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9-11) calls `recentEntries(all, 20)`, creates `new Array<string>(20)`, and writes `out[i] = page[i]` for every `i < page.length`. With more than 20 entries, `out` grows past 20 and the feed is no longer capped at one page. For a negative `limit`, the old `slice(0, -n)` dropped the last n entries, so returning `[]` there is also a behavior change, though a minor one.

findings.title: Entry-count header counts stale entries that are filtered out
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff filters stale entries out of `rows` (src/manifest.ts:20-21) but leaves `headerLines(opts, entries.length)` unchanged at line 22. For 5 entries with 2 stale, the header says `# entry-count: 5` and only 3 rows follow. `headerLines` writes `# entry-count: ${count}` at line 15, and that count is meant to describe the entries listed. Any consumer that validates or trusts the count (truncation checks, parsing) will see a mismatch.

findings.title: execute() unconditionally throws, removing its behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation returned `input.toUpperCase()`. The head replaces it with `throw new Error("always fails")`. The function is exported and has a `string` return type, and it now fails for every input. Any caller, including external consumers of the exported function, gets an exception instead of a result. The diff has no feature flag, no conditional and no explanation that would make this intentional.

findings.title: isEligible rejects viewers, making handle's read-only path dead
findings.whyItBreaks: The only caller of isEligible is handle (src/handler.ts:24). Before this change, an active viewer with attempts < 5 passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only" at line 25. The new `req.role === "viewer"` guard at line 18 makes isEligible return false for every viewer, so handle returns "rejected" first. The "read-only" branch at line 25 can no longer be reached. Viewers are a legitimate, handled role, and the existing branch shows the code meant to accept them with read-only handling.

findings.title: Payment check in shared canProceed blocks saving unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: `canProceed` at src/policy.ts:7 gates both `submitOrder` (src/actions.ts:4) and `saveDraft` (src/actions.ts:9). Payment is a legitimate precondition for submitting, but not for saving a draft. Before this change, `saveDraft({state:"draft", payment:"missing"})` returned "saved". Now `payment === "paid"` is false, so `canProceed` returns false and `saveDraft` returns "blocked". An unpaid draft is the normal state of a draft, so drafts can effectively no longer be saved until they are paid.

findings.title: Snapshot files come from 'stable' head, not the published channel
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot's `commit` is `repo.headCommit(channel)`, but `files` is now `repo.filesAt(stable)`, where `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")`. For any channel other than "stable", such as the default "main", the snapshot reports one commit and the file list of another. Consumers get a wrong, internally inconsistent manifest. If the "stable" ref doesn't exist, `headCommit("stable")` is an extra call that can fail, so publishing a valid channel can fail too. Nothing else in the repo uses `stable`, and the diff gives no reason for it.

findings.title: build() accepts `limit` but still hard-codes 10 results
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `limit=10` to the public `build` signature, which reads as a cap on the number of items. The body never reads it. `max_count = 10` on line 2 still drives `range(max_count)` on line 4. `build('x', limit=3)` returns 10 items, and `build('x', limit=50)` also returns 10. A caller who passes `limit` gets the wrong result, and nothing reports the mismatch.

findings.title: parse_positive_int does not enforce positivity
findings.whyItBreaks: The new name `parse_positive_int` promises that only positive integers are returned. The body is still `return int(value)`, so 0 and negative values pass through. `charge` (src/validators.py:6) now reads as if its input is validated, but `charge(-5)` returns -500 and `charge(0)` returns 0. `total_cents` then sums these, so a negative amount silently reduces the billed total. Before the rename the name `read_int` made no such promise, so this is a new mismatch between name and behavior.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy; apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version worked on `df.copy()` and returned a new frame, leaving the input untouched. The head version assigns with `df.loc[...] = value` directly on the argument and returns that same object. Any caller that treats the return value as a new frame, or reuses the original `df` afterwards (for example to compare before and after, or to apply several mappings to the same base), now sees its input silently changed. The function is a public module-level function, so its non-mutating behavior is observable. A caller that passes a slice or view of another frame can also get SettingWithCopyWarning behavior or unintended writes to the parent frame. The diff gives no reason for dropping the copy.

findings.title: `parse_positive_int` promises positivity but accepts negatives and zero
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name says the result is a positive integer, but the body is still `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)`. It returns negative values unchanged ("-5" -> -5) and returns 0 for "0" and for any parse failure. `charge` at src/parse.rs:6 calls it and now reads as if it only sees positive amounts. For "-5" it returns -500, which is a negative charge. Callers trust the name rather than the body.

findings.title: Remove dbg!(items) that moves the Vec and breaks the build
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!` takes its argument by value and returns it. `items` is a `Vec<String>`, which is not `Copy`, so `dbg!(items);` moves it and drops the returned value. The next line, `items.len()`, then uses a moved value and fails with E0382, so the crate no longer compiles. If it did compile, `dbg!` would still print the whole vector to stderr on every call, in release builds too.

findings.title: changedPaths computed from 'latest' but fromRevision still reports pinned tag
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset interface (src/changeset.ts:7-8) says fromRevision is the revision the changed paths were computed against, and that consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly that revision. After this change, fromRevision is store.resolve(pinnedTag), but changedPaths is store.readChangedPaths(latest), where latest is store.resolve("latest"). Whenever "latest" differs from the pinned tag, changedPaths describes changes relative to a different base than the one reported. A consumer replaying them on the pinned revision will skip changes made between the pinned tag and latest, or apply the wrong set of paths. When the two revisions are equal the result is the same as before.

findings.title: Column rename leaves src/query.sql selecting dropped `email` column
findings.whyItBreaks: The migration at migrations/0002_rename.sql:1 renames users.email to users.contact_email. The consumer at src/query.sql:1 still runs `SELECT email FROM users;`. After 0002 is applied, that query fails with 'no such column: email'. The diff doesn't update the query.

findings.title: Remove hardcoded live billing API key from source
findings.whyItBreaks: The line commits a `bk_live_...` credential to version control. Anyone with read access to the repo, its history, forks, or build artifacts can use it against the live billing API. It also stays in git history after a later revert, so the key must be treated as compromised and rotated. The change also removes the `BILLING_API_KEY` env lookup and the fail-fast `throw` when it is unset. Every environment (dev, test, staging, prod) now silently uses the live key, and operators can no longer rotate or override it without a code change. A misconfigured deployment no longer fails loudly. It sends live billing traffic instead.

findings.title: Inverted admin check lets non-admins purge archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code purged only when `user.isAdmin && project.archived`. The new code returns "forbidden" when `user.isAdmin` is true. A non-admin (`isAdmin=false`) skips that line. If the project is archived, the function then reaches `db.delete(project.id)` and returns "purged". Admins can no longer purge, and any user can permanently delete archived projects. This is an authorization bypass with data loss.

findings.title: startup() crashes with TypeError on a missing config file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() still returns None when the path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The diff removed the `settings is None` fallback in startup(), so `settings["workers"]` at app/config.py:14 now raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`. Before this change, a missing config file returned 1 worker. Deployments that have no config file, and any caller that relied on the default, now fail at startup. The error does not say that the config file is missing.

findings.title: Charge swallows gateway failure and returns nil
findings.whyItBreaks: When gw.Submit returns an error, the old code returned `charge failed: %w`. The new code only calls log.Printf and falls through to `return nil`. Any caller that checks `err == nil` will treat a declined or failed payment as successful. It may then fulfil an order, mark an invoice paid, or skip a retry. The only remaining signal is a log line. The `%w` wrapping is also lost, so callers can no longer use errors.Is or errors.As on gateway errors such as declined cards or timeouts. Only the `cents <= 0` validation error is still returned.

findings.title: Include tenantId in settings cache key to prevent cross-tenant leakage
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) returns `settings:${name}` with no tenant component, and settingsFor still fetches with store.fetch(tenantId, name). The first tenant to request a setting populates the shared module-level cache. Every later tenant requesting the same name gets a cache hit and receives the first tenant's value without calling the store. Example: tenant A reads 'billing_email' and gets a@x.com; tenant B then reads 'billing_email' and also gets a@x.com. This leaks data across tenants and returns wrong config. invalidate(name) also changed to a tenant-less signature, so it can no longer invalidate a single tenant's entry. It now clears the one shared entry for all tenants.

findings.title: Race in reserve: stock read before await, written after
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads `remaining` at line 15, checks it at line 16, then awaits `store.save` at line 17 before updating the in-memory map at line 18. While that await is pending, a second reserve(sku) call sees the same unchanged stock. For example, with stock=1, two concurrent calls both pass the `<= 0` check and both return true, so one unit is reserved twice. With stock=5, two concurrent calls both save 4 and both set 4. That loses one decrement and persists the wrong count to the Store. The previous synchronous version was atomic, so this regression comes from the diff. If save() rejects, the map is left unchanged, so the in-memory state stays consistent on failure.

findings.title: backoff() unit change breaks retry.ts, which still multiplies by 1000
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed from returning seconds (min(30, 2**attempt)) to returning milliseconds (min(30000, 2**attempt*1000)). src/net/poll.ts was updated to drop its `* 1000`. src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, and sleep takes ms. Attempt 0 now sleeps 1000 ms * 1000 = 1,000 s (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s. The cap becomes 30,000 * 1000 ms = 30,000 s (~8.3 h) instead of 30 s. Every retry() caller effectively hangs after its first failure.

findings.title: Propagate f.Close() error from Save instead of discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code returned f.Close()'s error on the success path. The new `defer f.Close()` at line 13 drops it, and `return w.Flush()` at line 20 returns nil whenever the flush succeeds. Close can fail on NFS, quota-exceeded and delayed-write filesystems, and that failure means the data was not durably written. Save is exported, so every caller gets nil for a file that may be truncated or missing data. Callers can't tell this apart from a real success. In the base, the error reached the caller through `return f.Close()` at the end of Save. Now it reaches nothing.

findings.title: Fix off-by-one in page_window that drops last row of each page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval, but the loop at lib/pagination.py:28 iterates range(start, end - 1). That skips the last row of every page. With rows=[a,b,c,d] and page_size=2, page 0 yields [a] instead of [a,b], and page 1 yields [c] instead of [c,d]. A page with one row yields an empty list. The old code used range(start, end). render_page (lib/pagination.py:40) and summarize therefore silently omit rows from the rendered output, and the numbering shows gaps where the dropped rows were. This is a data-loss regression in the output, and the refactor was meant to preserve behavior.

findings.title: Restore TTL comparison so fresh entries are returned
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was changed from `< ttlMs` to `> ttlMs`. A fresh entry (age < ttl) now fails the check, so it is deleted and `null` is returned. An expired entry (age > ttl) passes the check, so its stale value is returned. Every cache hit becomes a miss and expired data is served. The only exception is an entry whose age is exactly ttl, which is deleted.

findings.title: Avoid splicing the array while iterating in pruneDone
findings.whyItBreaks: `splice` inside `forEach` shifts the remaining elements left, but the iteration index keeps advancing. The element right after each removed job is skipped. For `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]`, the second done job is never examined and stays in the result. The function also now mutates the caller's array in place, where the old `filter` returned a new array. Any caller that kept a reference to the original list sees it change.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores sort
findings.whyItBreaks: `scores.sort()` with no comparator sorts numbers by their string form, and `.reverse()` then flips that order. For scores [5, 10, 100] the string order is ["10","100","5"] and the reversed order is [5, 100, 10]. With n=1, `topPlayers` takes cutoff = scores[0] = 5, so every player passes the filter and `slice(0,1)` returns the first player by input order, not the top scorer. Negative scores and mixed digit lengths are misordered the same way. The base code used `(a, b) => b - a`, so this is a regression introduced by the diff. `formatBoard` (line 20) calls `topPlayers`, so it displays the wrong board too.

findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook HMAC verification
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() at app/webhook.py:10 gates handle() (app/webhook.py:14), which returns 401 or runs the processor. The diff replaces hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) with a plain `==` on the hex HMAC digest. Python string `==` short-circuits at the first differing character, so response time can depend on how many leading characters of the attacker-supplied signature match. This gives a timing oracle on the authentication check, which could be used to forge webhook calls. The change has no functional benefit.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside the transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block. Now only `_record_ledger` is inside it (app/transfer.py:22-23). `_apply_balances` runs after the block exits (app/transfer.py:24), so the ledger insert has already been committed. If the debit UPDATE or the credit UPDATE fails, the ledger row stays committed but the balances are not updated. If the debit succeeds and the credit fails, money is removed from the source account and never credited. The two UPDATEs are also no longer atomic with each other. This is financial data corruption.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to host-local date components
findings.whyItBreaks: The base used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate. The head uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate (day.ts:4), which read the process's local timezone. The same instant now maps to different billing days depending on the TZ of the host. For example, 2026-03-01T02:00:00Z is 2026-03-01 in UTC but 2026-02-28 on a UTC-5 host. Usage near midnight UTC is therefore attributed to a different day than before, and also differs between hosts or containers with different TZ settings. sameBillingDay (day.ts:8) inherits this change, since it calls billingDay on both dates. Existing day keys that were computed in UTC will no longer match newly computed keys. The change is presented as a refactor, with no stated intent to change timezone semantics.

findings.title: Include tenant in profile memo key to avoid cross-tenant leak
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff changes the memo key from `${tenant}:${account}` to just `account` at src/profile.ts:14. `memo` is a module-level Map shared by all callers. `Profile` has a `tenant` field, and `fetchProfile` takes both tenant and account. If tenant A reads account 'alice' first, the profile is cached under 'alice'. A later `readProfile('B', 'alice', ...)` hits the cache at line 16 and returns tenant A's profile without calling `fetchProfile`. This leaks data across tenants whenever two tenants share an account id.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw `missing: <key>` when the key was absent. The new try/catch wraps a throw that it raises itself, then maps it to "" with a bare catch that neither logs nor rethrows. `load` is exported, so every caller now gets "" for both a missing key and a legitimately stored empty string. `loadAll` (src/store.ts:12) now returns "" entries for absent keys, where it used to fail fast. The catch also hides any other exception, such as a bad `store` argument.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows final failure and timeout expiry
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported retryBackground() catches every error with `catch { continue; }`. If all `config.retries` attempts fail it returns `void` as if it had succeeded. The `Date.now() > deadline` early return also exits silently. If `retries` is 0 or negative, `fn` is never called and the function still returns normally. A caller cannot tell success from exhausted retries, a deadline hit, or `fn` never running. The last error is never rethrown, logged, or returned.

findings.title: Config rename and new required field break existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Config renames `timeoutMs` to `timeout` and adds a required `retries` field that retry() never reads (src/retry.ts:8-9). Existing typed callers passing `{maxAttempts, timeoutMs}` fail typechecking. Untyped or JS callers pass no `timeout`, so `Date.now() + undefined` is NaN. `Date.now() > NaN` is always false, so retry() silently loses its deadline and runs all maxAttempts with no time bound. retry() callers must now supply an unrelated `retries` value.

findings.title: Field renders 'len=N' instead of the value, and number values break
findings.whyItBreaks: The input's `defaultValue` changed from `value` to the string `len=${value.length}`. Every consumer now sees `len=5` in the input instead of the actual value, so the component no longer shows or edits its data. The same change widens `value` to `string | number`, but `number` has no `.length`. `value.length` fails to type-check, and at runtime a number gives `undefined`, so the input shows `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Do not echo secrets.TOKEN to the workflow log
findings.whyItBreaks: The step exports secrets.TOKEN into the environment and runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, so the secret value is passed to stdout in the build log. GitHub masks exact matches, so the log normally shows `***`. Masking can be bypassed if the value is ever transformed, and the echo gains nothing. The workflow runs on `on: push`, but pushers already have write access and can edit the workflow themselves, so this adds little exposure over the baseline. It is still a needless secret-handling pattern that is easy to remove.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() spawnSync; 1MB default breaks large PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The change removes `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` from the git() helper, so spawnSync falls back to Node's default of 1 MiB. `git diff mergeBase headSha` (line 140) returns the full patch through this helper. When the patch is larger than 1 MiB, which a lockfile, generated file or vendored change easily causes, spawnSync kills the child with ENOBUFS. `res.status` is then null, so the `!== 0` check throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty message because stderr is empty. The throw happens in runGithub before the try/catch around review() (which starts at line 176). The uncaught error means no Needlefish check-run is posted and the action crashes. This is a regression, because the gh()/ghText() helpers in the same file still set 64MB, and git() did too until this change.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd set to the repo under review (src/shared/codex.ts:22-24) and passes the prompt on stdin. The prompt contains untrusted diff and PR content, so it is a prompt-injection surface. The old args pinned `-s read-only`. The new args drop it, so the sandbox now comes from the user's Codex config or profile (for example `sandbox_mode` in ~/.codex/config.toml). A config of workspace-write or danger-full-access would let an injected instruction in the reviewed diff modify the repo or run arbitrary commands. Nothing else in the repo enforces the sandbox. `rg` found no other `sandbox` or `read-only` reference.

findings.title: Restore merge-base when diffing against env-provided PR_BASE_SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code ran `git merge-base baseSha headSha` and diffed from that commit. The new code runs a two-dot `git diff baseSha HEAD` (line 139) and passes `baseSha` to `changedFileSet`, which runs `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` (line 57). `baseSha` comes from `process.env.PR_BASE_SHA`, which is typically the base branch tip. If the PR branch is behind the base, the two-dot diff also contains the reverse of every commit that landed on base after the branch point. Those changes then show up in `patch`, `changedFiles` and `changedPaths`. Findings can be raised against code the PR never touched, and `inlineComments` (line 61) accepts them because `changedPaths` is inflated. The diff also reads `HEAD`, while the review is anchored to `headSha`, which may be `PR_HEAD_SHA`. If the checkout is not the PR head, the reviewed content and the reported SHA differ.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid `$` pattern expansion in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The base used `() => ...` replacers, which insert the text literally. The change passes plain strings, and `String.prototype.replace` interprets special sequences in a string replacement: `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$$`. The replaced values are `JSON.stringify(bundle)`, `JSON.stringify(candidate)` and `bundle.patch`. The raw patch routinely contains these sequences, for example shell `$&`, `$'...'` and `$$`, and `` $` `` in JS template code. `$&` would be replaced by the matched placeholder text, and `` $` `` and `$'` would splice in the surrounding prompt text. `$$` would collapse to a single `$`. `$n` stays literal here because the pattern is a string with no capture groups. The diff the reviewer and critic see is therefore silently altered. This happens exactly on diffs that touch string-replace, regex or shell code, which are the diffs that need careful review. Nothing errors, so the review output is just wrong. The same applies to the bundle, since `agentsMd`, PR metadata and file paths can contain `$`.

findings.title: Fallback review post drops commit_id pin to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary POST sends `commit_id: headSha` in its JSON payload, which is the SHA that was diffed and reviewed. The fallback POST used to send the same pin (`-f commit_id=${headSha}`) but the diff removes it. Without `commit_id`, GitHub attaches the review to the PR's current head. The fallback runs whenever the primary call throws, for example when an inline comment line is not in the diff and returns 422. If the PR gets a new push while Needlefish is running, the fallback review (REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT) lands on an unreviewed commit. The check run in `postCheck` is still pinned to `headSha`, so the review and the check now refer to different commits. A stale REQUEST_CHANGES can then block a commit that never had the finding, or a PASS comment can be shown against code that was not reviewed.

findings.title: normalizeFinding swallows malformed findings into fabricated defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw on an invalid severity, an invalid category, a missing file, title, whyItBreaks or suggestedFix, and a non-positive or non-finite lineStart or lineEnd. normalizeReview also offered a non-strict mode that dropped bad findings. The new code maps every one of these to a default. An invalid or missing severity becomes "P1". An invalid category becomes "bug". A missing title becomes "Untitled finding". A missing file becomes "". A missing lineStart becomes 0. Missing whyItBreaks and suggestedFix become "". A non-numeric lineStart becomes NaN, because Number("abc") is NaN. A finding like `{}` or `{severity:"banana"}` now comes out as a plausible P1 "bug" finding with no file or line. Callers cannot distinguish it from a real finding. normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:131) maps findings through normalizeFinding with no way to tell a default from a real value. Its envelope validation is still strict, but the per-finding validation and the `strict` flag are gone, so there is no way to drop bad findings and keep the good ones. Both functions are exported, so this failure-to-default contract applies to every external caller.

findings.title: Restore -R/GH_REPO for gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step is the first step in the job, so it runs before `actions/checkout`. `gh pr view` without `-R` (and with no `GH_REPO` env var set) has to infer the repo from a local git remote. On a fresh or clean workspace there is no git repo, so gh errors with 'not a git repository'. If the self-hosted workspace keeps a stale checkout, gh could instead resolve against whatever remote that checkout has. The failure is hidden because the gh call sits inside `$(...)` within `echo`, so the step still exits 0 and writes `head=` and `base=` as empty outputs. The `Checkout PR head` step then gets `ref: ''` and checks out the default branch instead of the PR head. The review then runs against the wrong code, or against a diff with empty SHAs. The `workflow_dispatch` path, which relies on this else-branch, is affected.

findings.title: normalizeReview maps malformed review output to an empty clean review
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code threw 'malformed review output: ...' when raw was not an object, or when summary, findings, checked or residual_risks had the wrong type or was missing. The new code replaces each of those failures with a default: findings=[], residual_risks=[], checked=[], summary="". This applies to null, a string, {}, an error payload, and truncated or garbled JSON from the model. `normalizeReview(null)` and `normalizeReview({})` both return a well-formed RawReview with zero findings and zero blocking residual risks. The function is exported, so external consumers can no longer tell 'reviewer failed or returned garbage' from 'reviewer found nothing'. The changed lines show a forced default return in place of the removed throws. A wrongly typed `findings` is worse, because real findings are silently dropped. There are no in-repo callers (rg found only the definition), so the defect is the public contract itself.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch reviews the dispatch ref and passes empty PR SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow still offers `workflow_dispatch` with a required `pr_number` and says it bypasses the pull_request webhook. The removed `Resolve PR refs` step was the only thing that resolved the PR's head and base SHAs for that event, using `gh pr view`. Now, on dispatch, `github.event.pull_request.*` is empty. The checkout `ref` falls back to `github.ref`, which is the branch the workflow was dispatched on (e.g. main), not the PR head. `PR_BASE_SHA` and `PR_HEAD_SHA` are exported as empty strings. `--pr <n>` is still passed, so the CLI is asked to review PR N against a tree that is not that PR's head. Because the repo reviews itself, `src/cli.ts` also comes from the wrong tree. The `Fetch base branch` step defaults to `main`, so it fetches the wrong base for PRs that target another branch.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer for git() so large diffs don't fail
findings.whyItBreaks: The 64 MiB `maxBuffer` was removed from `git()`. Node's `spawnSync` then uses its 1 MiB default. `git()` is called at line 100 as `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"])`, which returns the entire patch on stdout. If the patch exceeds 1 MiB (lockfile updates, generated files, vendored code, large refactors), `spawnSync` kills the child and sets `res.error` to ENOBUFS. `res.status` is then null, so line 12 throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty or misleading stderr. Local review of any large PR fails with a confusing error. `gh()` at line 36 still sets 64 MiB, so the two helpers are now inconsistent.

findings.title: Dispatch path runs fork PR code on self-hosted runner with write token
findings.whyItBreaks: The job `if:` at line 24 only blocks fork PRs for the `pull_request` event. It is `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' || head.repo == repository`, so any `workflow_dispatch` run passes whatever `pr_number` is given. The `Resolve PR refs` step (lines 26-41) takes the head SHA from `gh pr view` without checking which repo it comes from. That SHA can belong to a fork PR. Before this diff the PR head was checked out into `target/` and treated as data only. Install and `src/cli.ts` came from `frankekn/needlefish@main`. Now the PR head is checked out into the workspace root (lines 43-47). `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 51) runs the PR's package.json and dependency lifecycle scripts. `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 59) then runs the PR's own code. Both steps run on a self-hosted runner in a login zsh. The review step also has `GH_TOKEN` with `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`. A maintainer dispatching a review of a fork PR therefore runs arbitrary contributor code on the runner machine. That was safe before this diff. Same-repo PRs can also now change the reviewer that judges them. That follows from the self-review design and is limited to authors with write access.

findings.title: Severity normalization removed; unrecognized severities now downgrade to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code did String(raw.severity).trim().toUpperCase() before checking membership, so 'p0', 'p1' and ' P2 ' were recovered to the right severity. The new code checks raw.severity verbatim, so those values fail the check and become 'P3'. The fallback for missing or garbage severity also moves from P1 to P3. A critical finding with a case or whitespace variation is therefore silently reported as low-severity, and the result looks like a real value, so callers cannot tell it from a genuine P3. normalizeReview (schema.ts:132) feeds every model-emitted finding through this function, and LLM output often varies in case.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing for the codex subprocess env
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code copied process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawning codex. The diff drops that, and spawnSync now inherits the full parent environment. codex runs against an untrusted repo and diff, with the prompt fed on stdin. Read-only sandbox mode blocks writes, but it does not stop the model from running something like `printenv` or `env`. A prompt injection in the PR content could therefore get the model to read the token and echo it into the last message or stdout. runCodex returns that text to the caller, so the token could end up in review output or comments. The diff gives no reason for removing the deliberate hardening.

findings.title: Restore fork guard: fork PRs execute untrusted code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only gate keeping fork PRs off this job. Without it, any fork PR triggers the job on `runs-on: self-hosted`. The job checks out the fork's head SHA (line 23). It then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28), which executes the fork's dependency lifecycle scripts and can resolve dependencies from the fork's lockfile. Finally it runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34), which is the fork's own code. That gives an arbitrary contributor remote code execution on the maintainer's machine, in a login zsh shell (`zsh -l {0}`) with that user's environment. GitHub normally gives fork PRs a read-only token and no secrets, but that does not protect the runner host, its filesystem, its credentials or its network. Self-hosted runners should not run fork PR code.

findings.title: Explicit 0 duration is now silently replaced by the default
findings.whyItBreaks: `readRunnerDurationMs` used to accept 0 (`parsed >= 0`). Now `parsed > 0` sends "0" to the fallback. 0 is meaningful for both callers. `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` means SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM (lines 118-124), and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` means stop waiting for `close` at once (lines 120-123). After this change, setting either to 0 gives 5000 ms or 2000 ms instead, with no error or warning. An operator cannot tell their setting was ignored. The function is exported, so its behavior contract (non-negative values accepted) also changed. Nothing in the diff explains the change.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks are dropped before the critic and verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code collected `res.residual_risks` from every deep pass into `residuals` and passed them to the critic as `candidateMerged.residual_risks`. The head code never reads `res.residual_risks` and hardcodes `residual_risks: []` at src/core/review.ts:113. A deep reviewer can report `blocks:true` ('could not verify X'), and that signal now stops at the deep pass. The critic never sees it, `pruned.residual_risks` can come back empty, and `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` at src/core/review.ts:122 can return PASS.

findings.title: Removed coverage backstop lets changed files go unreviewed with no signal
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code added a tail hotspot for every changed file not in a selected hotspot. The head code has no backstop: `.slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` at src/core/review.ts:93 keeps at most 6 hotspots. Any file the map pass left out, or put only in a dropped hotspot, is never deep-reviewed. The loop at src/core/review.ts:97 iterates only those hotspots. Nothing records the skipped files as a residual risk, so the review can return PASS for a large diff that was only partly read.

findings.title: formatDuration emits 60s / Nm 60s near minute boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: The minutes value is floored from raw ms, but the seconds value is rounded separately. When ms % 60000 >= 59500, the rounded seconds equal 60 and the carry into minutes is lost. For ms=59600 the old code gave totalSeconds=60 and '1m 0s'. The new code gives minutes=0, seconds=round(59.6)=60 and '60s'. For ms=119600 the new code gives '1m 60s' where the old code gave '2m 0s'. Both formatted outputs are rendered in the stage and total timing lines (src/shared/render.ts:75,80).

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 and empty/blank strings
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function is named parsePositiveInteger, and its error message says "requires a positive integer". After the change the guard is `parsed < 0`, so 0 passes. Number("") and Number("   ") both evaluate to 0, so an empty or blank CLI/env value is now silently accepted as 0. Before the change the `<= 0` check rejected all of these. Any external caller that uses the result as a timeout, retry count, or divisor gets 0 instead of a validation error. I found no in-repo callers, so the damage is limited to the public contract itself, which no longer does what its name and error text say.
